en: Majjhima Nikāya 60: The Discourse on the Incontrovertible (Apaṇṇakasutta).
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large community of monks, arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Sālā.
The brahmin householders of Sālā heard:
"The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakya clan, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large community of monks, has arrived at Sālā."
Furthermore, this excellent report of Master Gotama’s fame has spread abroad:

“Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having personally realized this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans, through his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then the brahmin householders of Sālā approached the Blessed One; having approached, they...
Some, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One;
having concluded the polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side.
Some, having extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Some [sat] in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having announced their names and clans, some sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence.
As the brahmin householders of Sāleyyaka were sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to them:
"Householders, do you have any teacher who is pleasing to you, in whom you have acquired a reasoned faith?"
“Venerable sir, we have no teacher who is pleasing to us, toward whom we have acquired a well-founded faith.
“Householders, since you have not found a pleasing teacher, this infallible Dhamma should be undertaken and practiced by you.
For when the infallible Dhamma is fully mastered and undertaken, it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.”
And what, householders, is the incontrovertible Dhamma?
There are, householders, some recluses and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view:
“There is no giving, there is no offering, there is no sacrifice; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done.”
‘There is no result of kamma; there is no this world, nor a world beyond; there is no mother, nor a father;

there are no beings who arise spontaneously; and there are no ascetics or brahmins in the world who have attained the right path and practiced rightly, who having realized this world and the world beyond for themselves through direct knowledge, make it known.’”
Householders, among those very ascetics and brahmins, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak in direct opposition.
They say this:
“There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed, there is what is offered; there is the fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done.”
‘There is kamma and its result; there is this world and the other world; there is mother and father; there are beings of spontaneous birth;

and there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have fared rightly and practiced rightly, who have realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge and make them known.’”
“What do you think, householders:
‘Are these ascetics and brahmins not proponents of diametrically opposed views to one another?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“In this regard, householders, as for those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view:

‘There is no giving, there is no offering... [as before] ...those who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make it known’—it is to be expected of them that they would not practice these three things:
good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.”
Having turned away from wholesome states, they will adopt and practice these three unwholesome states: misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
And for what reason?

For those venerable recluses and brahmins do not see the danger, the degradation, and the defilement of unwholesome states, nor the benefit, the aspect of purification, and the renunciation inherent in wholesome states.
Although the next world exists, they hold the view: "There is no next world"; this is their wrong view.
Furthermore, although the next world exists, they intend: "There is no next world"; this is their wrong intention.
Indeed, when the other world exists, he speaks the words, "There is no other world"; this is his wrong speech.
Indeed, when the other world exists, he says, "There is no other world"; he opposes those who are arahants and knowers of the other world.
Indeed, when the other world exists, he convinces another that "there is no other world"; this is his persuasion toward what is not the true Dhamma.
And by that persuasion toward what is not the true Dhamma, he exalts himself and disparages others.
Thus, his former virtue has been abandoned and immorality has arisen;
this is wrong view, wrong intention, and wrong speech, an opposition to the noble ones, and persuasion toward what is not the true Dhamma.
Self-praise and disparagement of others—in this way, these many evil, unwholesome states arise with wrong view as their condition.
In this regard, householders, a wise person reflects thus:
“If indeed there is no other world, then at the breaking up of the body, this person will make himself safe.”

"If there indeed is a world beyond, then this person, upon the breakup of the body after death, will be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell. But even granting that there is no world beyond,
and that the words of these venerable recluses and brahmins are true, nevertheless,
this person is censurable by the wise in this very life as an immoral person, one of wrong view, and a nihilist."
If indeed there is a world beyond, then for this person there is a double failure:
that he is censured by the wise in this very life, and that after the breakup of the body, after death, he will reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell.
Thus this unerring doctrine, though poorly undertaken and poorly adopted, stands pervading one side only; it leaves aside the wholesome state.
In this regard, householders, as for those recluses and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view:

‘There is what is given... [and so on]... those who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make it known’—it is to be expected of them that they will abandon these:
bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.
Having avoided these three unwholesome states, they will undertake and practice these three wholesome states: good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.
For what reason?

For those worthy recluses and brahmins perceive the danger, the degradation, and the defilement of unwholesome states, as well as the benefit of renunciation and the side of purification in wholesome states.
Since there actually is another world, they hold the view: "There is another world"; this is their right view.
Since there actually is another world, they intend: "There is another world"; this is their right intention.
Indeed, when the other world exists, one speaks the words, “The other world exists”; this is one’s right speech.
Indeed, when the other world exists, one says, “The other world exists”; one does not oppose those arahants who know the other world.
Indeed, when the other world exists, one convinces another that “the other world exists”; this is one’s instruction in the true Dhamma.
And by means of that exhortation to the true Dhamma, he neither extols himself nor disparages others.
Thus, his immorality has already been abandoned and his virtue is established—this right view, right intention, and right speech;

this non-opposition to the noble ones, this exhortation to the true Dhamma, this lack of self-exaltation, and this lack of disparagement of others. In this way, these many wholesome states arise with right view as their condition.
In this regard, householders, a wise person reflects thus:
"If indeed there is another world, then upon the breakup of the body, after death, this person will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
But even if there is no other world, let the word of these venerable recluses and brahmins be true."
And yet, this venerable person is praised by the wise in this very life as a virtuous person with right view who maintains the doctrine of the afterlife.
If indeed there is a world beyond, then for this venerable person there is success in both respects:
that he is praised by the wise in this very life, and that upon the breakup of the body, after death, he will reappear in a happy destination, a heavenly world.
Thus this infallible Dhamma of his, well-perfected and undertaken, stands pervading both sides; it leaves behind the unwholesome state.
Householders, there are some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“For one who acts or causes to act, who cuts or causes to cut, who cooks or causes to cook, who grieves or causes to grieve, who tires...”
For one who causes exhaustion, for one who trembles or causes others to tremble, for one who takes life, for one who takes what is not given,
for one who breaks into a dwelling, for one who carries off plunder, for one who commits robbery, for one who lies in ambush, for one who goes to another's wife, or for one who speaks falsehood—
no evil is committed by such a doer.

Even if one were to use a wheel the size of a chariot felly to turn all the living beings on this earth into a single heap of flesh, a single mass of flesh, there would be no evil resulting from that, nor any consequence of evil.

Even if one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges killing and causing to kill, mutilating and causing to mutilate, cooking and causing to cook, there would be no evil resulting from that, nor any consequence of evil.

"Even if one were to go to the further bank of the Ganges giving gifts and causing others to give, making offerings and causing others to offer, there would be no merit resulting from that, nor any arrival of merit. Through giving, self-control, restraint, and the speaking of truth, there is no merit, nor any arrival of merit. ‘For one who acts and causes others to act; who cuts and causes others to cut; who cooks and causes others to cook;
who grieves and causes others to grieve; who tires and causes others to tire; who trembles and causes others to tremble;
who takes the life of a living being, takes what is not given, breaks into dwellings, plunders by ambush, commits burglary, lies on the highway, commits adultery, and speaks falsehood—’
For one who speaks, for one who acts, evil is performed.

Even if one were to use a wheel with razor-sharp edges to turn this earth into a single heap of flesh, a single mass of flesh, there would be evil resulting from that; there would be the accrual of evil.

Even if one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges killing and causing to kill, cutting and causing to cut, cooking and causing to cook, there would be evil resulting from that; there would be the accrual of evil.
‘Even if one were to go along the northern bank of the Ganges, giving and causing others to give, sacrificing and causing others to sacrifice—on that account there would be merit;
there would be an acquisition of merit. Through giving, self-control, restraint, and truthful speech, there is merit;
there is an acquisition of merit. What do you think, householders?
“Are not these ascetics and brahmins proponents of diametrically opposed views to one another?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”—
“In that regard, householders, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:”
‘For one who acts and causes others to act; who cuts and causes others to cut; who cooks and causes others to cook;
who grieves and causes others to grieve; who tires and causes others to tire; who trembles and causes others to tremble;
who takes the life of a living being, takes what is not given, breaks into dwellings, plunders by force, commits robbery, ambushes highways, commits adultery, and speaks falsehood—’
"For one who speaks thus, for one who acts thus, no evil is committed.

Even if, with a wheel whose edge is as sharp as a razor, one were to reduce all living beings on this earth to a single heap of flesh, a single mass of flesh, there would be no evil on that account, nor any consequence of evil.

And even if one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges killing and slaughtering... [and so on] ...there is no merit, nor any consequence of merit, through giving, self-control, restraint, or the speaking of truth."
For them, this is to be expected: having abandoned these three wholesome states— namely, good conduct of body,
good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind— they will persist in undertaking these three unwholesome states— namely, misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
For what reason?

Because those worthy recluses and brahmins do not see the danger, the degradation, and the defilement in unwholesome states, nor the blessing of renunciation and the side of purification in wholesome states.
Although action exists, they hold the view: "There is no action"; this is their wrong view.
When there is indeed action, one intends that "there is no action"; this is his wrong intention.
When there is indeed action, one speaks the words "there is no action"; this is his wrong speech.
When there is indeed action, one says "there is no action," thereby opposing those arahants who maintain the doctrine of action.
Furthermore, while an action is actually present, he convinces others that "there is no action"; this is his persuasion toward what is not the true Dhamma (*asaddhamma-saññatti*).
By means of that persuasion toward what is not the true Dhamma, he exalts himself and disparages others.
Thus, his prior virtue has been abandoned and non-virtue has become manifest.
And this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, opposition to the noble ones, incitement to unrighteousness,
self-exaltation, and disparagement of others— thus these many evil, unwholesome states arise with wrong view as their condition.
In this regard, householders, a wise person reflects thus:
‘If there is no kamma, then this person, upon the breakup of the body, will make himself safe;
but if there is kamma, then this person, upon the breakup of the body after death, will reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
However, let there be no kamma; let the words of these venerable recluses and brahmins be true.’
And yet, this venerable person is censured by the wise in this very life as "an immoral person, one of wrong view, a proponent of non-doing.
If there truly is such a thing as doing, then this venerable person has made a bad choice in both respects:
that he is censured by the wise in this very life, and that after the breakup of the body, after death, he will reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
Thus this infallible Dhamma of his is poorly grasped and undertaken; it remains partial, neglecting the wholesome state.
In this regard, householders, those recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as:
‘For one who acts or causes to act, who cuts or causes to cut, who cooks or causes to cook, who grieves or causes to grieve, who exhausts... [the result follows].
For one who causes exhaustion, for one who trembles or causes others to tremble, for one who takes life, for one who takes what is not given, for one who breaks into a dwelling,
for one who carries off plunder, for one who commits robbery, for one who stands as an ambusher, for one who goes to another’s wife,
and for one who speaks falsehood— evil is done by such a person.

Even if one were to grind all the living beings on this earth into a single mass of flesh, a single heap of flesh, with a wheel as wide as a threshing floor, there would still be evil resulting from that; there would be the arrival of evil.

Even if one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges killing and causing to kill, cutting and causing to cut, cooking and causing to cook, there would still be evil resulting from that; there would be the arrival of evil.
Even if one were to go along the northern bank of the Ganges giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, there would still be [merit] resulting from that.
‘There is merit; there is the acquisition of merit. Through giving, self-control, restraint, and the speaking of truth, there is merit;
there is the acquisition of merit’—it is to be expected that they will abandon these things: bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.”
Having avoided these three unwholesome states, they will undertake and practice these three wholesome states: good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.
For what reason?
For those worthy recluses and brahmins perceive the danger, degradation, and defilement of unwholesome states, and the benefit, the side of purification, and renunciation in wholesome states.
Since action truly exists, they hold the view: "Action exists"; this is their right view.
Since action truly exists, they intend: "Action exists"; this is their right intention.
When there is indeed action, he speaks the words, “There is action”; this is his right speech.
When there is indeed action, he says, “There is action”; he does not oppose those arahants who are proponents of action.
When there is indeed action, he convinces another that “there is action”; this is his persuasion toward the true Dhamma.
And by means of that exhortation to the true Dhamma, he neither praises himself nor disparages others.

Thus, his immorality has already been abandoned and his virtue is established—this right view, right intention, and right speech, as well as non-opposition to the noble ones, exhortation to the true Dhamma, lack of self-praise, and lack of disparagement of others: in this way, these many wholesome states arise with right view as their condition.
In this regard, householders, a wise person reflects thus:
‘If indeed there is action, then upon the breakup of the body, after death, this person will reappear in a happy destination, a heavenly world.
But even if there were no action, let the words of these venerable recluses and brahmins be true.’”
And yet, this venerable person is praised by the wise in this very life as "a virtuous person of right view who maintains the doctrine of action.
If indeed there is such a thing as action, then this venerable person has gained an advantage in both respects:
that he is praised by the wise in this very life, and that with the breakup of the body, after death, he will reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
Thus this infallible Dhamma of his, well-perfected and undertaken, stands pervading both sides and leaves behind the unwholesome state.
Householders, there are some recluses and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view:
"There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings."
Beings become defiled without cause and without condition.
There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings;
beings are purified without cause and without condition.
“There is no power, there is no effort, there is no human strength, there is no human prowess;

all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are powerless, devoid of strength, devoid of effort, subject to the transformation of destiny, chance, and inherent nature, and they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth.
Now, householders, some ascetics and brahmins among those very ascetics and brahmins hold views that are diametrically opposed to this.
They spoke thus:
"There is a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings;
with cause and with condition, beings become defiled."
There is a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings;
with cause and with condition, beings are purified.
There is power, there is energy, there is human strength, there is human exertion.

‘Not all beings, not all living creatures, not all existents, not all souls are without mastery, without power, without energy, but are transformed by destiny, chance, and inherent nature, and thus experience pleasure and pain within the six classes of birth.
What do you think, householders,
are these ascetics and brahmins not proponents of doctrines that are directly opposed to one another?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In this regard, householders, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as this:
‘There is no cause, there is no condition, for the defilement of beings;’”
Beings become defiled without cause and without condition.
There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings;
beings are purified without cause and without condition.
‘There is no power, there is no effort, there is no human strength, there is no human exertion;
all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are powerless, devoid of strength, devoid of effort, subject to the transformation of destiny, chance, and nature,
and they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth.’”

For them, this is to be expected: having avoided these three wholesome states— namely, good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind— they will persist in undertaking these three unwholesome states— namely, misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
For what reason?

Because those worthy recluses and brahmins do not see the danger, the degradation, and the defilement in unwholesome states, nor the benefit of renunciation and the side of purification in wholesome states.
Although there actually is a cause, they hold the view that "there is no cause"; this is their wrong view.
When there is indeed a cause, one conceives the thought, "There is no cause"; this is his wrong intention.
When there is indeed a cause, one utters the speech, "There is no cause"; this is his wrong speech.
When there is indeed a cause, one says, "There is no cause"; he opposes those Worthy Ones who teach the existence of causes.
Furthermore, when there actually is a cause, he convinces others that "there is no cause";
this is his persuasion toward what is not the true Dhamma. By means of that persuasion toward what is not the true Dhamma, he exalts himself and disparages others.
Thus, his prior virtue has been abandoned, and non-virtue is present.
And this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, opposition to the noble ones, the incitement to unrighteousness,
self-exaltation, and the disparagement of others— in this way, these many evil, unwholesome states arise with wrong view as their condition.
In this regard, householders, a wise person reflects thus:
"If there is no cause, then this person, with the breakup of the body after death, will make himself safe;
but if there is a cause, then this person, with the breakup of the body after death, will reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
However, let there be no cause; let the words of those venerable recluses and brahmins be true."
And yet, this venerable person is censured by the wise in this very life as ‘an immoral person, one of wrong view, a proponent of causelessness.
If there truly is a cause, then this venerable person has made a bad choice in both respects:
that he is censured by the wise in this very life, and that after the breakup of the body, after death, he will reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell.
Thus this infallible Dhamma of his is poorly grasped and undertaken; it stands pervading only one side and neglects the wholesome state.
In this regard, householders, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as:
‘There is a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings;’
Beings become defiled with causes and conditions.
There is a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings;
beings become purified with causes and conditions.
“There is power, there is vigor, there is human strength, there is human exertion; it is not the case that all beings, all living things, all creatures,
all souls are powerless, devoid of vigor, and subject to the transformation of destiny, chance, and inherent nature,
experiencing pleasure and pain within the six classes of birth.”
It is to be expected of them that, having avoided these three unwholesome states— namely, misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind—
they will undertake and abide in these three wholesome states— namely, good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.

And why is that? Because those worthy recluses and brahmins see the danger, degradation, and defilement in unwholesome states, and they see the benefit of renunciation and the side of purification in wholesome states.
Since the cause truly exists, he holds the view: "The cause exists"; this is his right view.
When there actually is a cause, one intends, "There is a cause"; this is his right intention.
When there actually is a cause, one speaks the words, "There is a cause"; this is his right speech.
When there actually is a cause, one says, "There is a cause"; thus one does not contradict those Worthy Ones who teach the doctrine of causality.
Furthermore, when one correctly informs others that a cause truly exists by saying, "There is a cause," this is an instruction in the true Dhamma.
By means of that instruction in the true Dhamma, one neither exalts oneself nor disparages others.
Thus, his immorality has been abandoned beforehand, and virtue is established.

And this right view, right intention, and right speech—non-opposition toward the noble ones, compliance with the true Dhamma, not exalting oneself, and not disparaging others—in this way, these many wholesome states arise with right view as their condition.

In this regard, householders, a wise person reflects thus: "If there is indeed a cause, then this person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world."
Granted, there may be no cause; let the words of these venerable recluses and brahmins be true.
Nevertheless, this person is praised by the wise in this very life as a virtuous person of right view who maintains the doctrine of causality.
If indeed there is a cause, then this venerable person has gained a double advantage.

That which is praised by the wise in this very life, and that which, upon the breakup of the body, after death, one will be reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world—thus this infallible Dhamma of his is well-perfected and undertaken;
it stands pervading both sides and leaves behind the unwholesome state.
Householders, there are some recluses and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view:
‘There are no formless realms at all.
Now, householders, some ascetics and brahmins among those very same ascetics and brahmins hold views that are diametrically opposed;
they speak as follows:
‘There are entirely formless realms.
What do you think, householders,
are these ascetics and brahmins not proponents of mutually contradictory views?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In this regard, householders, a wise man reflects thus:
‘Those worthy recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:’”
‘There are no formless realms at all’— this has not been seen by me;
and as for those venerable recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as ‘There are formless realms at all’— this has not been understood by me.
If I, not knowing and not seeing, were to take one side and declare:
"Only this is true, anything else is false," that would not be fitting for me.
As for those worthy recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
‘There are no formless realms at all’— if the word of those venerable recluses and brahmins is true,
it is possible that I shall certainly be reborn among those gods who possess form and are mind-made.
But as for those venerable recluses and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view:

‘The formless realms exist in every respect. If the word of those venerable recluses and brahmins is true, it is possible that I shall certainly be reborn among those gods who are formless and made of perception.
For it is seen that on account of form there arise the taking up of sticks, the taking up of weapons, quarrels, strife, disputes, contention, slander, and false speech.
‘But this does not exist at all in the formless realm.
Having reflected thus, he practices for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of forms themselves.
Householders, there are some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“There is no cessation of existence whatsoever.
Now, householder, among those very same ascetics and brahmins, some ascetics and brahmins hold diametrically opposed views and say this:
‘There is a complete cessation of existence.
What do you think, householders,
are these ascetics and brahmins not proponents of mutually contradictory views?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In this regard, householders, a wise person reflects thus:
‘Those worthy recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:’”
‘There is no cessation of existence in every respect’— this has not been seen by me;
and as for those worthy recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as ‘there is a cessation of existence in every respect,’ this has not been understood by me.
If I, not knowing and not seeing, were to take one side and declare:
"Only this is true, anything else is false," that would not be fitting for me.
As for those venerable recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
‘There is no cessation of existence whatsoever’— if the word of those venerable recluses and brahmins is true,
it is possible that I shall certainly be reborn among those gods who are formless and made of perception.
But as for those venerable recluses and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view:
‘There is a complete cessation of existence’— if the words of those venerable recluses and brahmins are true,
it is possible that I shall attain final Nibbāna even in this very life.
As for those venerable recluses and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view:
‘There is no cessation of existence in every respect’—for those who hold such a view, this view is close to passion, close to bondage, close to delighting, close to clinging, and close to grasping.
But for those venerable recluses and brahmins who speak thus and hold the view:
‘There is cessation of existence in every respect’—for them, this view is close to non-passion, close to non-bondage, close to non-delight, close to non-clinging, and close to non-grasping.
Having reflected thus, he practices for the sake of disenchantment with existences, for their fading away, and for their cessation.
Householders, there are these four types of persons found existing in the world.
Which four?
"Householders, here a certain person is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of tormenting himself.
Householders, here a certain person is a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
Householders, here a certain person is both a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of tormenting himself, and a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others."
"Householders, here a certain person does not torment himself nor is he devoted to the practice of self-torment, nor does he torment others nor is he devoted to the practice of tormenting others.

Being neither a tormentor of self nor a tormentor of others, in this very life he is free from hunger, extinguished, become cool, experiencing happiness, and dwells with a self that has become sublime.
And what, householders, is the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment?"
"Householders, here a certain person goes naked, rejecting conventions, licking his hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked...
[as above] ...he dwells engaged in such various practices of self-torment and self-mortification.
This, householders, is called a person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself."
"And what, householders, is the person who torments others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others?
Here, householders, a certain person is a butcher of sheep, a butcher of pigs... or whatever other cruel occupations there may be.
This, householders, is called the person who torments others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others."
And what kind of person, householders, is one who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others?
Here, householders, a certain person is a consecrated kṣatriya king...
[and so on] ...they perform their services while threatened by punishment, threatened by fear, with tearful faces, weeping.
This, householders, is called the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and who also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
And what, householders, is the person who neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of self-torment, nor torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others;
who, neither tormenting himself nor tormenting others, is in this very life hungerless, extinguished, become cool, experiencing happiness, and dwells with a self that has become sublime?
In this case, householders, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha...
[as before] ...having abandoned these five hindrances, which are defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom.

Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first *jhāna*, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second *jhāna*, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration.
… [and so on] … the third *jhāna* … [and so on] …
He enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say, one birth, two births... [as far as] thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their karma.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
He understands as it really is: “This is suffering” ... [and so on] ...
he understands as it really is: “This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints.”
For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the taint of existence, and the mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance.
When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: "It is liberated.
One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."

“Householders, this is called the person who neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of torturing himself, and who neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of torturing others;
who, neither tormenting himself nor tormenting others, is in this very life free from hunger, extinguished, become cool, experiencing happiness, and dwells with a self that has become sublime.
When this was said, the brahmin householders of Sālā said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!

Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the path to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has Master Gotama made the Dhamma clear in many ways.”
"In this very way, Master Gotama has elucidated the Dhamma in many ways.
We go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Gotama accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."
The Apaṇṇaka Sutta, the tenth, is finished.
The first chapter, the Chapter on Householders, is finished.
Here is its summary verse:
And Kandaranāgarasekhavat,
then Potaliya, the servant of Jīvaka;
Upāli, and then Kukkura and Abhaya.
The tenth is from the Bahuvedanīya-apannaka.
